Actually, no—Albert Einstein was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921**, but **not for the theory of relativity**. Instead, he received the prize **"for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect."**

This might be surprising, given how famous the theory of relativity is, but at the time, the photoelectric effect was considered more definitively proven and revolutionary in its own right. Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect—showing that light could behave as particles (later called photons)—was a foundational contribution to quantum theory.

While Einstein's work on special and general relativity was widely recognized as groundbreaking, it was still considered somewhat controversial or not fully verified at the time (especially general relativity). So, the Nobel Committee chose to honor his work on the photoelectric effect, which had strong experimental support.

So in short: **No, Einstein did not win the Nobel Prize for relativity**—he won it for the photoelectric effect.
